explanations.answer: To be confident and unashamed before Him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says to remain in Christ "…so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming." Notice he doesn't say nervous, and he doesn't say hiding behind the couch. I think he wants them walking up with their heads up.

explanations.answer: To be the very first ones He greets
explanations.explanation: Nope, the text never mentions a greeting line. It says he wants them confident and unashamed before Him at His coming. I think that's a better deal than being first anyway. Nobody has to elbow anybody at the front of the line.

explanations.answer: To be given more than everyone else
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say anything about getting more than anybody else. What he wants for the little children is that they be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming. That's about how they stand before Him, not a bigger box of cookies than the next baker's. And his word to them is to remain in Christ.

Right on the money. The writer says, "If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him." So if somebody is practicing righteousness, the text says they've been born of Him. Simple as dough, flour and a little water.

Careful, friend, this one is true. The writer says, "If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him." That's the very thing you were asked about. Easy one to second-guess, and I second-guess my own recipes all the time.

Yes, ma'am, yes, sir, children of God! The writer says, "Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God." Look at the word "given." The Father's love is what He has given. My cookie cutter kids called me Papa, but this is a way bigger deal.

That's a nice-sounding title, but it's not the one the writer uses. He says the Father's love has given us this: "…that we should be called children of God." Servants isn't in the verse. Children is the word he picked.

The writer doesn't mention the prophets at all here. He points to the Father's love and says we should be "…called children of God." The name comes from the Father, not from who we hang around with. I'd take that name over any friend list.
This one's false, friend, and I'm glad. Right after "…children of God." the writer adds, "And that is what we are!" He doesn't say it's a nickname or a label stuck on a jar. He says it's what we are.

Yes! The text says we should be called children of God, and then adds, "And that is what we are!" So it's not only a title. Then he says it again in verse 2: "…we are now children of God…" He says it twice, so I'm guessing he wants it to stick.

That's it, friend. The writer says, "The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him." Think about it like this: if you never met somebody, you won't recognize his kids at the grocery store. The world's trouble starts with not knowing Him, and that's why it doesn't know us.

The writer never says God's children are hiding anything. The reason he gives is this: "…it did not know Him." The world didn't know Him, so it doesn't know us. That one's about the world, not about anybody tucking their faith in a drawer.

The text doesn't say anything about the world not hearing. It says, "The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him." Hearing about somebody and knowing somebody are two different things. The writer is talking about the second one.

Yes! The writer says, "We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him…" That's the part that's still ahead. Right now the writer says we are children of God, and what we will be "…has not yet been revealed." But he knows this much, and he says it plain.
New names are a nice thought, but this verse doesn't say that. The writer says, "…when Christ appears, we will be like Him…" That's what we will be. Like Him is a lot bigger than a name tag.

That's not in this verse, friend. The writer says what we will be has not yet been revealed, but he does tell us one thing: "…when Christ appears, we will be like Him…" I won't add anything he didn't say. Like Him is already plenty.

explanations.answer: They will see Him as He is
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The writer says, "…we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is." The word "for" is the reason right there in the verse. Seeing Him as He is comes with being like Him.

explanations.answer: They will hear His voice call them
explanations.explanation: That's a lovely picture, but the text doesn't say it here. The reason the writer gives is, "…for we will see Him as He is." It's about seeing, not hearing. Keep your eyes open on this one.

explanations.answer: They will sit at His table with Him
explanations.explanation: A table sounds right at home in my bakery, but the writer doesn't say it in this verse. His reason is, "…for we will see Him as He is." That's what comes with being like Him. I'll stick with what the verse gives.

Pure is the word. The writer says everyone who has this hope "…purifies himself, just as Christ is pure." Christ is the standard, not the neighbor down the street. And the hope is what he points to right before it, that we will be like Him.

Patient is a good word, but it's not the one in this verse. The writer says everyone who has this hope "…purifies himself, just as Christ is pure." Purifying and pure go together like a mixing bowl and a spoon. Pure is the one that fits.
Powerful doesn't show up in this verse. The writer says, "…purifies himself, just as Christ is pure." That's the comparison he makes. Purifies and pure are cousins, and powerful isn't in the family.
That's the one. The writer says, "Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well." Plain, no sugar on it. He doesn't tiptoe, and neither will I.

explanations.answer: He has only made a mistake
explanations.explanation: That's not how the writer puts it. He says, "Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well." A slip is one thing, but he's talking about practicing. And then he adds, "…sin is lawlessness."

explanations.answer: He is still learning the law
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say anything about learning the law. He says, "Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well." It's about what a person practices, not what they're still studying. He follows it with, "…sin is lawlessness."
Sins is right. The writer says, "…Christ appeared to take away sins…" Not just to point at them or to make a list. To take them away.
Sorrows is a good guess, since we all have some. But the verse says, "…Christ appeared to take away sins…" The writer is talking about sin here, so that's the word. Sorrows aren't in this sentence.

Sickness isn't the word in this verse, friend. The writer says, "…Christ appeared to take away sins…" Taking away means the sins get removed, not just noticed or put on a list. He's reminding them of something they already know, and he adds that "…in Him there is no sin." (1 John 3:5)

Yes, and the writer says it right after the other part. "…you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin." Not a speck. Those two things sit side by side in the same verse.
This one is true, friend. The writer says, "…in Him there is no sin." He says it in the same verse where Christ appears to take away sins. No sin in Him, none at all.

explanations.answer: He has not seen or known Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer says, "No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him." It's a serious line, so I'll say it plain and leave it there. It follows right after, "No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning."

explanations.answer: He is closer to Christ than he thinks
explanations.explanation: That's not what the writer says. His words are, "No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him." It's the opposite of closer. He's talking about someone who continues in sin.

explanations.answer: He only needs one more warning
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't mention a warning count here. He says, "No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him." That's the whole statement. I won't add anything he didn't.

Careful, this one's false. The writer says, "…let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous." It's about practicing righteousness, not just saying it. He doesn't say it doesn't matter how a person lives.

Yes, false. The writer warns, "…let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous." The righteous one is the one who practices it. A claim by itself isn't what he points to.
True, and I love this verse. The writer says, "This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil." It tells us why the Son of God was revealed. That's what He came to do.

This one is true, friend. The writer says, "This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil." Right before that, he says the devil has been sinning from the very start. So the Son of God was revealed to destroy what the devil has been doing.

That's it. The writer says, "…God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God." So it's tied to being born of God. The seed abiding in him is the reason the verse gives.

explanations.answer: The fear of judgment holds him back
explanations.explanation: Fear isn't what the writer points to here. He says, "…God’s seed abides in him…" That's the reason, along with having been born of God. Nothing about being scared of anything.

explanations.answer: His temptations have all gone away
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The writer says anyone born of God refuses to practice sin "…because God’s seed abides in him…" That's the reason he gives. He doesn't say anything about temptations going away.

explanations.answer: He does not love his brother
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the one. The writer says, "Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother." So he gives two signs of someone who is not of God. Not practicing righteousness is the first, and not loving his brother is the one you picked.

explanations.answer: He does not know the law
explanations.explanation: That's not the sign the writer gives. He says, "Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother." The second sign is about love for a brother. Knowing the law isn't in the verse.

explanations.answer: He does not keep the feasts
explanations.explanation: Feasts aren't mentioned in this passage, friend. The writer says, "…nor is anyone who does not love his brother." That's the second sign, right after not practicing righteousness. Love for his brother is the one.
